human_tolerance.notes: Feeds in cow pastures, sometimes visits backyard bird feeders, and favours croplands after harvest to scavenge seeds on the ground; can adapt to virtually any dense native plant community as long as coverage and openings are widely available.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Courtship begins during March and April, when the birds are still flocked together in winter areas. Males are polygamous and may court in groups, the dominant male gobbling, strutting with spread tail feathers, drumming/booming and spitting.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: When mating is finished females search for nest sites: shallow dirt depressions engulfed with woody vegetation. Hens lay a clutch of 10-14 eggs, usually one per day, which are incubated for at least 28 days.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Poults are precocial and nidifugous, leaving the nest in about 12-24 hours, and are observed eating insects, berries and seeds.

vocalizations.description: In early spring, males older than a year old gobble to announce their presence to females and competing males; the gobble can be heard up to a mile away. Gobbling is reduced in some seasons by pressure, precipitation and temperature.

One of a large repertoire of calls that also includes the assembly call, plain yelp, purr, cluck, cutt, excited yelp, fly-down cackle, tree call, kee kee run and putt; males also give a low-pitched drumming or booming sound produced by air moving in the chest air sac, and a sharp 'spit'.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives family Phasianidae, order Galliformes and authority Linnaeus, 1758; ITIS scientific-name search returns TSN 176136 with the same authority. Linnaeus described it in the 1758 tenth edition of Systema Naturae with type locality Mexico.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 9606290 from species/match; ITIS TSN 176136 from the ITIS scientific-name search; NCBI taxon id 9103, eBird code wiltur and IUCN category least concern (Q211005) from Wikidata P685, P3444 and P141.

range.note: 'The wild turkey is an upland game bird native to North America' with type locality Mexico, described as the ancestor to the domestic turkey derived from a southern Mexican subspecies. The country list covers the United States, Canada, Mexico and the Central American countries named in the species' published range; it is recorded at country level and read as approximate.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'Wild turkeys are omnivorous, foraging on the ground or climbing shrubs and small trees to feed'; 'Despite their weight, wild turkeys, unlike their domesticated counterparts, are agile, fast fliers ... They usually fly close to the ground for no more than 400 m.'

traits.nest_type.note: 'Nests are shallow dirt depressions engulfed with woody vegetation' and 'Turkeys are a ground nesting bird, and because of this they are heavily preyed on'.

traits.perching.note: 'at twilight most turkeys will roost well off the ground in trees for safety' and they shelter in conifer trees during blizzards; perching is true, though the source also says they usually fly no more than 400 m.

traits.senses.note: From the Flight section: 'Wild turkeys have very good eyesight during the day. However, their vision is very poor at night', which gives vision_color true and night_vision false. hearing High from the large vocal repertoire and the male's use of calls for social dominance. olfaction Low is authored; the source notes turkeys benefit from the deer's 'improved olfactory sense' as a sentinel, implying their own is not the strong sense.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: the size_class bands are Tiny under 0.05 kg, Small under 1 kg, Medium under 50 kg and Large at 50 kg and above, so a 7.6 kg adult male is Medium. That reads oddly for an animal the source calls 'the heaviest member of the order Galliformes' and 'among the heaviest flying birds in the world', but the schema's bands have no separate class for very large birds, so Medium is the value the data actually supports rather than a squeezed-in Large.

traits.mass_kg.note: 'Per two large studies, the average weight of adult males is 7.6 kg'. The male mean is used because the model shows an adult male, identifiable by its beard, strutting display and red-white-blue head.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Females typically 2.5-5.4 kg and males 5-11 kg; the range spans the species, from the lightest typical hen to the heaviest typical tom.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the adult male range 100-125 cm.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Authored from AVONET: the tarsus, the leg segment from the ankle to the ground, measures 9.7-19.1 cm, so 0.6 m is an order-of-magnitude standing height for an adult male with long sturdy legs. The source does not state a shoulder height and no open source consulted gives one, so this is a judgement, not a measurement.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Judgement, and an honest gap: the Wikipedia article states only that 'Beards grow continuously during the turkey's lifespan' and gives no longevity figure, and no openly licensed source consulted states a mean or typical lifespan for this species. 8.0 years is an authored order-of-magnitude figure for a large game bird with a high adult survival rate. Treat it as a placeholder, not a measurement.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-PlantO 40, Diet-Inv 20, Diet-Fruit 20, Diet-Seed 20. PlantO is split here across the schema's mast, seed, fruit and browse fields because the source itemises the plant diet precisely: 'They prefer eating acorns, nuts, and other hard mast of various trees, including hazel, chestnut, hickory, and pinyon pine, as well as various seeds, berries such as juniper and bearberry, buds, leaves, fern fronds, roots, and insects.' The record sums to 1.0; the browse share is small because buds, leaves and fern fronds are a minor part of a diet centred on mast, seeds and berries.

traits.social.note: Flock is the primary year-round structure from 'when turkeys are still flocked together in winter areas' and 'Turkey populations can reach large numbers in small areas'; 'Males are polygamous, mating with as many hens as they can' describes the breeding system, and males may also court in pairs of close relatives. The upper bound of 20 is an authored figure, since the source says only 'large numbers'.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'Early morning and late afternoon are the desired times for eating', with the male gobbling in early spring and the flock roosting in trees at twilight; diurnal, with poor night vision.

traits.defense.note: Authored: the species is heavily preyed on as a ground nester, and its documented responses are fleeing and flushing to distance rather than fighting; the male's strutting, drumming and spitting are display and dominance signals, not defence.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: a heavily hunted game bird with good daytime eyesight that roosts in trees away from danger, but one that also 'sometimes visit[s] backyard bird feeders' and feeds in open cow pastures, so a middling-to-high value is used.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-ground 90; ForStrat-understory 10 mapped to arboreal, matching the described tree roosting and the climbing of shrubs and small trees to feed.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: the day roost is high in a tree and the night roost is 'well off the ground in trees', with shelter in conifers during blizzards; shrub_thicket reflects the dense thickets used for shelter and nesting in the source's habitat accounts, and the tree roost is carried as a perch resource.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet. Nesting weight 1.0 on nest_ground follows the nest description. Perch and shrub_thicket shelter weights are authored judgement; no open source quantifies their relative use.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'Wild turkeys often feed in cow pastures, sometimes visit backyard bird feeders, and favor croplands after harvest to scavenge seeds on the ground', plus 'They seemingly can adapt to virtually any dense native plant community as long as coverage and openings are widely available.' light_max is authored (judgement).

seasonal.phases.note: Mating window from 'Courtship begins during the months of March and April'; nesting from 'When mating is finished females search for nest sites' with a 10-14 egg clutch incubated at least 28 days; the young window follows the precocial, nidifugous poults leaving the nest in 12-24 hours. Exact window edges are judgements informed by those dates.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg duration from 'The eggs are incubated for at least 28 days' (28 used, the stated minimum). The juvenile stage carries a scale but no duration: the source gives no age at which poults reach adult size, and inventing one would be dishonest, so the field is left unset.

vocalizations.gobble.note: From the Vocalizations section, including the audibility ('up to a mile away'), the seasonal trigger ('In early spring, males older than a year old ... gobble to announce their presence to females and competing males') and the weather effect.

vocalizations.yelp.note: The source names and lists the species' whole call repertoire (assembly call, gobble, plain yelp, purr, cluck, cutt, excited yelp, fly-down cackle, tree call, kee kee run, putt) plus the drumming/booming and the spit, but does not describe any individual call except the gobble. The description here is therefore an authored summary of the repertoire, and 'plain yelp' is used as the alarm because it is the contact and alarm call the source lists, not because the source assigns it that role.

vocalizations.note: The gobble description is sourced; the yelp description is an authored summary as noted in its own entry. Months, time windows and cooldowns are authored judgement, since no open source quantifies them. No frequency bands are given, so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the Description and display sections: 'Fully-grown wild turkeys have long, reddish-yellow to grayish-green legs', 'Their heads and necks are colored with red, white, and blue', 'Females have feathers that are duller overall, in shades of brown and gray', 'The primary wing feathers have white bars', and the male's display of 'spreading out their tails'. The head and beak are coloured from the accent slot for the bare red head and neck, the tail from the markings slot for the dark barred fan, and a beard part renders the male's breast tuft. The model shows an adult male. Proportions are authored judgement for a long-legged, short-winged, small-headed galliform with a high girth. The torso girth and leg length were also reduced once from a first pass that rendered as a deep barrel on short legs, which did not read as a galliform; the model shown is the second pass.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program, which is the only perching-bird program available and the closest fit for a large ground-walking bird that roosts in trees and has a loud seasonal display call. food_tag set to mast, the preferred food. flee_m raised to 30 m for a large, wary, ground-foraging bird that flushes to trees. song and alarm point at the documented gobble and yelp. nest_m1/nest_m2 set to the April-June nesting season. Note that the program is written for a small hopping songbird, so its ground-foraging-by-hops detail does not match a walking galliform; a bespoke program would fit better but is not written here, and that limitation is left visible rather than hidden.
